news.2026-11-12-panama-canal-hegseth-con: Panama Canal: Pete Hegseth says the United States “controls” it together with Panama, which replies that it belongs to Panamanians alone

On Tuesday, November 10, at the Pentagon, U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said that Washington and Panama now jointly control the canal, after pushing China aside. On Wednesday the 11th, Panamanian Foreign Minister Javier Martínez-Acha replied that only Panama runs this key route for world trade [1][2][4].

At a press briefing at the Pentagon, Pete Hegseth said: “Panama has set aside China’s efforts, and now, together with them, we control the canal” [2][5]. He added: “This is our hemisphere and we are acting accordingly” [4].
According to the press, he was linking this to Panama’s exit from the “New Silk Roads,” China’s vast infrastructure program [2][5].

On Wednesday, Javier Martínez-Acha replied: “No country other than ours has control over the administration of the Panama Canal,” and recalled that the canal “is operated and administered by Panama” [1][3].

The minister explained that the security agreements with the United States cover the fight against drug trafficking, organized crime and threats to critical infrastructure, and that they transfer neither sovereignty nor control [1][2]. Panama has similar cooperation arrangements with the United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, Colombia and Spain [1][4].

Javier Martínez-Acha refused to engage in a “rhetorical competition” with a foreign official and said he wanted a “calm, firm, diplomatic and sovereign” response; according to him, José Raúl Mulino’s government does not want to get involved in rivalries between great powers [2][5].

President José Raúl Mulino also rejected these claims and defended Panamanian sovereignty over the waterway, handed over by the United States at the end of 1999 [5][6]. Lawmaker Patsy Lee pointed out that the Constitution entrusts management of the canal to the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) [4].

Key takeaway: the question of who controls the Panama Canal is back in the spotlight, and Washington presents it as a victory over China. For Panama, it is a red line: the Constitution reserves management of the canal for its national authority [2][4].

The canal is vital for the United States: during a previous visit to Panama, Pete Hegseth said that 70% of the ships using it are headed to or coming from U.S. ports [7]. That is why Washington closely watches any Chinese presence around ports and infrastructure [7].

Panama is walking a tightrope: it cooperates with the United States on security, but refuses to have that cooperation presented as shared management [1][3]. By distancing itself from “rivalries between great powers,” its government is trying not to become a battleground between Washington and Beijing [2].

For you, the Panama Canal matters even far from the Americas: it is a shortcut between the Atlantic and the Pacific for world trade. Any tension over how it operates can lengthen shipping routes and make transport more expensive, and therefore some imported goods too.

news.2026-11-12-chili-recession-techniqu: Chile: the finance minister acknowledges a “technical recession” for the first time, dragged down by the slump in copper

On Wednesday, November 11, in an interview with Bloomberg, Jorge Quiroz, finance minister under President José Antonio Kast, admitted that Chile was in a technical recession. The cause: a collapse in copper production. He also opened the door to private capital in Codelco, the state-owned copper giant [1][4][5].

A technical recession is when gross domestic product (GDP, the wealth produced) shrinks for two quarters in a row [6]. Jorge Quiroz described it as “a snapshot of things that happened over the last two quarters” and said: “You can call it a recession” [1][5].
According to the minister, the main cause is the drop in copper production, while non-mining sectors continue to grow [1][4].

The monthly economic activity indicator (Imacec) fell 1.5% in July and 1.0% in August year on year, before a small 0.2% rise in September; for the year, the economy is contracting by 0.4% [3][4]. In September, mining output fell 12.1% [4].
Unemployment stands at 9.8%, according to figures cited by the Chilean press [4].
Jorge Quiroz says the recession “has already hit people” but that consumption is recovering, and forecasts growth close to 3% in 2027 [2][4].
On Codelco, he supports keeping state control, but says he is open to long-term private capital and to selling non-strategic assets [1][4].
According to The Clinic, this would be the country’s fifth recession after four previous ones, from the Asian crisis to the pandemic; the official third-quarter figure has not yet been published [3].

Key takeaway: it is rare for a government to use the word “recession” itself, and it shows how dependent Chile is on its copper. When the mines produce less, the whole economy shrinks, even if the rest of activity is growing [1][4].

How it works: in September, mining output plunged 12.1% year on year, and that sector alone was enough to drag overall growth down to 0.2% [4]. For the year as a whole, the economy has slipped into the red, at −0.4% [4].

The admission comes as the government of José Antonio Kast, in power for eight months, is piling up crises, according to the Chilean press [7]. By opening the debate on private investment in Codelco, Jorge Quiroz is touching a national symbol [1].
What comes next will depend on copper: the minister is betting on a return to growth close to 3% in 2027, and the press also cites a target of 4% in 2028 [4].

For you, Chilean copper ends up in electric cables, electric cars and electronics. When Chile’s mines produce less, the global supply of copper tightens, which can eventually make products you buy more expensive.

United States: the House buries Pete Hegseth’s impeachment by seven votes, Democrats vow to return in January

The House of Representatives, still under a Republican majority, voted 211 to 204 to send back to committee the impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accused mainly over the war against Iran. The text is dead for this session, but Democrats, who will take over Congress in January, say “this is only the beginning” [1][2][3].

The vote took place on Tuesday, November 10: 211 members voted to refer Thomas Massie’s resolution to committee, against 204, which effectively buries it [1][3]. The text had been filed as “privileged,” which forced Republican leaders to hold a vote within two legislative days [2].

The resolution contained eight articles of impeachment: violation of the Constitution, unauthorized military operations and abuse of power, relating to the war in Iran and operations in Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean [1][3].
Thomas Massie, a representative from Kentucky, was the only Republican to vote against the referral; 18 members did not vote, including 7 Republicans and 11 Democrats [1][4].

Pete Hegseth denounced a “farce” and a “political stunt” and said he has no intention of resigning [2][3]. Donald Trump welcomed the fact that the attempt had “miserably FAILED” [2]. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries warned: “This is only the beginning” [2].
Thomas Massie, who leaves Congress in January, has given up on a new procedure and instead wants to force a vote on the president’s war powers [2][5].

In the Senate, Republicans re-elected John Thune as their leader, unopposed, even as they are about to lose the majority [6]. On the Democratic side, Bernie Sanders refuses to back Chuck Schumer as future majority leader [7].
The outgoing Congress must also pass a budget before December 11: none of the twelve spending bills has been adopted, and the federal government is running on a stopgap law [8].

Key takeaway: Pete Hegseth stays in office, but the reprieve may be short. The vote came down to seven votes, and the new Democratic majority, elected on November 3, will be able to relaunch the procedure as early as January [1][3].

The heart of the case is the war against Iran: the resolution accused the secretary of conducting military operations without authorization from Congress [1][3]. It is the same question Thomas Massie now wants to raise with a vote on war powers [2].

These final weeks of the old Congress, known as the “lame duck” session, are busy: a shutdown of federal services after December 11 must be avoided, while Democrats are reluctant to give Donald Trump a “blank check” before they take power [8].

For you, the battle over the war against Iran is also being fought in the U.S. Congress: the more lawmakers constrain military operations, the more the chances of de-escalation around the Strait of Hormuz, and therefore of cheaper oil, may shift.

Bangladesh: more than 100 homemade bombs and buses set on fire as Sheikh Hasina’s announced return approaches

Since November 10, Bangladesh has been hit by a wave of violence: homemade bombs, buses and trains set on fire, a driver killed. Police blame the Awami League, the banned party of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was sentenced to death in absentia and whose return is announced for December [1][3][5][8].

During the night of Monday, November 9, to Tuesday, November 10, around 1 a.m., more than 100 homemade bombs exploded near the toll plaza of the Padma Bridge, in Shariatpur district, during a road blockade [3]. Hundreds of activists from the Chhatra League, the banned student wing of the Awami League, were blocking the road with logs and oars [10][7].
A bus driver was killed in Faridpur district, as bombings and vehicle arson spread to several districts [1][3].

In 24 hours, at least 22 vehicles were set on fire in 11 districts and at least 28 homemade bombs exploded in Dhaka and six other districts, according to one tally [6]. An Indian media outlet reports violence in 21 districts, with buses and trains set on fire [5].

In the capital, at least 15 homemade bomb explosions have been recorded since November 1, and at least 898 people linked to the Awami League have been arrested since that date [4]. Police say they have deployed 15,000 additional officers in Dhaka, with night patrols and checkpoints [7][8].

In Khagrachhari district, a local BNP office was set on fire during the nationwide blockade launched by the Chhatra League [7][8]. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed promises tough prosecution of those behind attacks on buses and public buildings [4][1].
According to police, people linked to the Awami League are involved in some of the attacks; these accusations have not been independently verified [1][4].

Sheikh Hasina, who has taken refuge in India, plans to return in December; a British law firm is seeking to recover her passport and identity card from the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi [8][2].
Key takeaway: Sheikh Hasina’s announced return is reigniting the war between her camp and the current authorities, with homemade bombs and vehicle arson in many districts [2][5].
Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia by the International Crimes Tribunal for crimes against humanity during the July 2024 uprising, and Dhaka is demanding her extradition from India [8].
Her return would therefore pose a dilemma: arrest her, at the risk of inflaming her supporters, or leave her free, at the risk of defying the courts; either way, tension is already rising [8][2].
The blockades target the country’s vital routes, such as the Padma Bridge or the Dhaka-Khulna highway, disrupting the movement of goods and workers [3][10][7].
For you, Bangladesh is one of the world’s major garment workshops: a lasting political crisis can delay deliveries and weigh on the prices of some T-shirts or jeans sold in France.

Uruguay: the port of Nueva Palmira offers landlocked Bolivia an outlet to the Atlantic at reduced rates

According to the Bolivian press on Wednesday, November 11, the Uruguayan port of Nueva Palmira presented an offer to Bolivian exporters in Santa Cruz, Bolivia: a reserved area in the port, preferential rates and special customs regimes. For Bolivia, which has no access to the sea, it is one more route to the Atlantic via the rivers [1][2][4].
Nicolás Suárez, harbor master of the port of Nueva Palmira, presented the proposal to exporters in Santa Cruz, Bolivia’s economic capital [2][3].

Bolivia has an enclave in the port, an area where its goods in transit are stored before being loaded onto larger ships [2][3]. The offer also includes special customs regimes and preferential rates [1][2].

According to Nicolás Suárez, Bolivian cargo pays lower rates than other operations, although the cost depends on the type of goods and services; some operations pay no wharfage fees [2]. The terminal has already handled 1.75 million tons in transit since the start of the year [2].
The route would start from Puerto Quijarro or Puerto Busch, in eastern Bolivia, by barge along the Paraguay-Paraná waterway, to Nueva Palmira, on the Río de la Plata [3].

This waterway raises concerns: Argentina, which manages it, has once again extended the international toll at $1.30 per net register ton, with the initial rate of $1.47 suspended, and Paraguayan shipowners fear changes after the tender [5].

Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz describes Uruguay as his country’s “sixth border” and links access to the sea to this waterway [6]. According to him, the Uruguay-Paraguay-Bolivia bloc (Urupabol) wants to triple barge transport capacity [7].
Yamandú Orsi’s Uruguayan government is also studying a deep-water port at Rocha, on the Atlantic, and hopes to decide on its feasibility in 2027 [8].

Key takeaway: Bolivia, which has no access to the sea, is looking for alternative outlets for its exports, and Uruguay is positioning itself as a partner. An enclave and reduced rates make the river route to the Atlantic more concrete [1][2].

How it works: goods travel down the Paraguay-Paraná waterway by barge, then are transferred to large ships at Nueva Palmira, avoiding transit through other neighbors’ ports [3]. The Urupabol bloc is also coordinating infrastructure to bring iron from Bolivia’s El Mutún deposit to the Atlantic [7].

There is also competition between ports: Uruguay wants to strengthen Nueva Palmira’s role on the waterway against Argentina, which sets the tolls [4][5]. Every cent per ton counts for heavy, low-value products such as grain or ores [5].

For you, these South American river routes carry soybeans, grain and ores sold all over the world. The more efficient and cheaper they are, the lower the cost at which these raw materials reach markets, including in Europe.

Eswatini: the kingdom shuts down foreign-owned shops and gives them 12 months to comply or leave

In Eswatini, a small kingdom in southern Africa, inspectors are closing shops run by foreigners, mostly Asian, under a new law on citizens’ economic empowerment. On Tuesday, November 10, lawmakers backed a 12-month deadline for non-compliant businesses to regularize or close [1][2][4][7].

The member of parliament for Mbabane East, Welcome Dlamini, told Parliament on November 10 that officials from the Ministry of Commerce had already started closing shops [5][6]. The inspections began in August 2026 [4][5].
These closures are based on the Citizen Economic Empowerment Act, which aims to reserve more business activities for Swazis [2][4].

Lawmakers backed a 12-month deadline for non-compliant foreign businesses to comply or close [1][3][6]. But until the law is amended to include this deadline, the ministry can continue to enforce it immediately [6][5].
The ministry says its inspections aim to identify violations, not to drive out all foreign businesses; some of the shops inspected, notably in Mbabane, were found to be compliant [5][7].
Hhohho lawmaker Tanele Magagula, on the contrary, is calling for the immediate seizure of foreign businesses in rural areas: “Why should we wait three years while emaSwati suffer?” [6][7].
The inspections also uncovered problems with working conditions: employees complain that rest days, annual leave and overtime are not respected [5][7].
Draft regulations presented in 2026 propose reserving retail businesses with annual turnover below 8 million emalangeni for citizen-owned companies [7][4].
Key takeaway: Eswatini joins the list of African countries that want to hand small retail back to their citizens, at the risk of tensions with the foreign communities that run it [4][7].
The rules remain unclear: a 12-month deadline backed by lawmakers does not have the force of law, and closures are continuing on the ground, creating great uncertainty for shopkeepers [6][5].
Pressure is also rising in neighboring South Africa, where campaigns against immigrants have led to raids, arrests, looting and closures of informal shops run by foreigners [5].

The debate pits two approaches against each other: protecting local shopkeepers from competition seen as unfair, or giving foreign businesses, some of them found compliant, time to avoid abrupt closures [6][7][5].

For you, this is a concrete example of a trend that also affects Europe: the temptation to reserve certain jobs for nationals. In a small country, closing foreign shops can push up prices and make goods scarcer in villages if local shopkeepers do not take over.

Czech arms group CSG falls as much as 23% on the stock market: it sold off old shells at a discount and is now worth less than half its IPO price

On November 11, Czech arms group CSG lowered its 2026 margin forecast from about 24-25% to 21%, after selling stocks of old ammunition at reduced prices. Its share price fell as much as 23% during the session and is now worth less than half its IPO price of €25 [1][2][3].
CSG now targets an operating margin (EBIT) of about 21% in 2026, compared with 24% to 25% announced previously; its revenue forecast remains €7.4 billion to €7.5 billion [2].
Third-quarter revenue fell to €1.51 billion, compared with €1.7 billion a year earlier, and came in below analysts’ expectations [1][4].
The reason given: to meet demand from customers who want extended-range shells, CSG sold off older, standard-range ammunition it had in stock at reduced prices [3][4].
The share lost as much as 23% during the session, hitting €10.35, before closing down 13.1% at €11.68, according to MLQ; it had peaked at €35.50 after listing at €25 [2][3].
According to Bloomberg, the stock fell to its lowest level since the IPO and is worth less than half the price paid by the first shareholders [1].
The bank Jefferies called the results “weak”: the new margin would put annual operating profit about 15% below the midpoint of analysts’ expectations; it nevertheless keeps a price target of €25 [3].
CSG maintains its medium-term targets and says its own long-range shell production will be ready by the end of 2027 [3].

Key takeaway: the war in Ukraine and European rearmament are no longer enough to lift defense stocks. Investors now look at the profitability of each contract, and weaker-than-expected profit is punished very hard [2][3].
CSG’s problem reveals a shift in demand. Armies want shells that fire farther; stocks of conventional shells are losing value and must be sold more cheaply until the new production is ready [3][4].

The drop is part of a losing streak for the sector. On November 5, Germany’s Rheinmetall had already lost more than 15% after a further cut to its forecasts, linked to the postponement of a major armored vehicle contract [5].
For the first shareholders, the loss is heavy: bought at €25, the stock was worth €11.68 at the close, despite still-strong European military demand [3].

For you, this drop is a reminder that a fashionable sector, like defense since 2022, can lose you a lot of money if companies disappoint on their margins. Many “European defense” funds hold stocks of this kind. This is not buy or sell advice.

Nissan sees its profit melt away by 96% and cuts its sales forecast again because of China: the stock loses 5% in Tokyo

On November 11, Nissan reported operating profit of just ¥2.1 billion (about $13 million) for July-September, 96% less than a year earlier, and cut its sales forecast once again. On Thursday, November 12, the stock lost 5.22% in Tokyo [1][2].
Operating profit for the quarter fell to ¥2.1 billion; analysts expected ¥54.9 billion according to FactSet, or ¥60.1 billion according to an LSEG poll cited by Reuters [1][2].
Three causes: the disappearance of a one-off benefit from last year linked to lower emissions costs in the United States, higher costs for raw materials and parts, and weak sales in China [2].
Nissan lowered its global sales forecast for the fiscal year ending in March 2027 to 2.97-3 million vehicles, from 3.15 million previously [1][6].
The carmaker nevertheless maintains its annual operating profit target of ¥200 billion [1][3].
In its statement, Nissan speaks of “progress” in the first half and confirms its financial forecasts; its CEO presented a plan to fight back, according to CNBC [1][4].
The stock lost 5.22% on Thursday in Tokyo and is down 29% since January [1].
The same day, the Nikkei index slipped 0.1% to 61,224.87 points, held back by concerns about Nvidia [7].

Key takeaway: Nissan is caught in a pincer between China, where its sales remain weak, and rising costs, notably in the United States, where a one-off benefit has disappeared. A quarter with almost no profit shows that its turnaround is still to come [1][2].
Keeping the ¥200 billion target is surprising: it assumes a much better second half. Investors have doubts, as the fall in the stock shows [1][3].
The contrast is stark with Toyota, whose stock jumped nearly 17% on November 5 after better-than-expected profit, its biggest rise in nearly forty years [9].
China, long a growth driver for Japanese carmakers, is becoming their weak spot: Nissan is cutting its sales forecast “again” because of its difficulties in China, CNBC points out [1].

How it works: why a carmaker’s profit can vanish quickly

A car factory is very expensive, whether it runs at full capacity or not: machines, wages, research. These are fixed costs. When sales fall, like Nissan’s in China, these costs remain and are spread over fewer cars [2]. If, on top of that, the price of parts and raw materials rises, the margin on each car shrinks [2]. The result: a small drop in sales can wipe out profit, here by 96% [1]. This is called operating leverage. It also works the other way: when sales pick up, profits rise quickly, which is what Nissan’s unchanged annual target assumes [3].
